379.title: Gargi returns: "two questions, like two arrows" — the imperishable (3.8)
379.hook: the woman who was silenced stands up again, like a warrior stringing a bow, with two questions
379.howItsDone: The akshara passage is studied in Vedanta as one of the Upanishads' great descriptions of Brahman by negation; Gargi's two questions are often retold in Hindu teaching as the moment the debate turns.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uddalaka asked about the thread and the inner controller, the one whose body the earth is. Your line was antaryamin.

Gargi stands up again. Two days ago she was told: don't ask too much, or your head will fall off, and she sat down. This time she speaks to the whole room first. Honored scholars, I'll ask him two questions. If he answers them, none of you will ever beat him. Then she turns to Yajnavalkya. As a warrior's son from Kashi or Videha strings his unstrung bow, takes two sharp arrows in his hand and rises to fight, so I rise against you with two questions. Answer them.
screen: `SHE STANDS UP AGAIN.` → `A WARRIOR STRINGING HIS BOW.` → `TWO QUESTIONS, LIKE TWO ARROWS.`

segments.voice: First arrow. What is above the sky and below the earth and between the two, what people call past, present and future: on what is that woven? On space, Gargi. She bows. Honor to you, Yajnavalkya, for that answer. Get ready for the second. Second arrow. And on what is space woven? This time he doesn't stop her. He answers. That, Gargi, is what the knowers of Brahman call the imperishable, the akshara. It is neither coarse nor fine, neither short nor long. Without shadow, without darkness. Without wind, without space. Without taste or smell, without eye or ear, without voice or mind, without breath or mouth, without measure, without inside or outside. It eats nothing, and nothing eats it. Then he says what it does. At the command of this imperishable, Gargi, the sun and moon are held apart. Earth and sky are held apart. Hours, days, months and years are held apart. Rivers run east from the snowy mountains, and others west. And whoever performs rites and austerities for thousands of years without knowing this, it comes to an end. Last time, Gargi asked what holds the worlds of Brahman, as if it were one more thing. This time the answer isn't a thing. It's described almost entirely by what it isn't. And Gargi turns to the room. Count yourselves lucky if you get away by bowing to him. None of you will beat him. And she falls silent, on her own terms.

380.title: Vidagdha Shakalya: how many gods? 3,306 → 33 → 6 → 3 → 2 → 1½ → 1 (3.9)
380.hook: the last challenger asks how many gods there are, and keeps asking until the number counts down to one
380.howItsDone: Hindu traditions hold many forms of the divine together with the conviction that the divine is one; ekam sad vipra bahudha vadanti from the Rig Veda is often quoted for that idea, and the thirty-three gods are named in Vedic ritual.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Gargi's two arrows drew out akshara, the imperishable, without inside or outside. Your line was neither coarse nor fine.

People sometimes say Hindus have three hundred thirty million gods. The Upanishad has its own count, and it's a countdown. The last challenger, Vidagdha Shakalya, asks Yajnavalkya: how many gods are there? Three thousand three hundred and six, he answers. Yes, says Shakalya. But how many gods are there, really? Thirty-three. Yes, but how many really? Six. Really? Three. Really? Two. Really? One and a half. And how many gods are there, really? One.

Then Shakalya makes him explain each number. The three thousand and more, Yajnavalkya says, are only their powers. There are really thirty-three: eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, twelve Adityas, and Indra and Prajapati. The Vasus are fire, earth, wind, the middle air, sun, sky, moon and stars: everything dwells in them. The Rudras are the ten breaths in a person, and the self: when they leave the body, they make people weep. The Adityas are the twelve months, carrying everything along. Indra is the thunder; Prajapati is the sacrifice. The six are fire, earth, wind, the middle air, the sun and the sky. The three are the three worlds. The two are food and breath. The one and a half? The wind that blows, because everything grows in it. It's a pun in Sanskrit; it doesn't translate. And the one? Breath. It is Brahman. They call it That. Notice what didn't happen: the countdown never says the many gods were a mistake. They fold onto one, like a fan folding shut. A verse in the Rig Veda says it in a single line: ekam sad vipra bahudha vadanti. Truth is one; the wise speak of it in many ways. Hindus live this in different ways. Some worship one form of God as supreme, and see the others as that God's forms or helpers. Others honor many deities, each in its place. Advaita teachers hear in the count one reality appearing as many. This passage gives all of them room.

381.title: Shakalya's head falls off (3.9)
381.hook: the debate's last challenger keeps pushing, and the warning that stopped Gargi comes true for him
381.tomorrow: Janaka and Yajnavalkya: what is the light of man?
381.howItsDone: The Vedic brahmodya, a formal contest of questions about Brahman, is the setting of this chapter; teachers of the Upanishads read Shakalya's end alongside Gargi's warning, and the closing tree verses end the third book with a riddle.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shakalya's countdown, from 3,306 gods all the way to one. Your line was one.

After the countdown, Shakalya doesn't sit down. He keeps firing questions: the gods of each direction, what the heart rests on, what the self is founded on. Yajnavalkya answers each one. Then, somewhere in the middle, he stops and asks Shakalya something. Shakalya, have these scholars made you their coal-tongs? Their tool for pulling hot coals out of the fire, so they don't burn their own hands?
screen: `HE DOESN'T SIT DOWN.` → `QUESTION AFTER QUESTION.` → `HAVE THEY MADE YOU THEIR COAL-TONGS?`

segments.voice: That line tells you what's going on. Shakalya isn't Gargi, chasing a question to its edge. The others have sent him in to do the burning work for them. And he keeps going. So at last Yajnavalkya turns the debate around. Now I ask you, he says, about the person taught in the Upanishads, the one who leads all these out, brings them back, and goes beyond them. If you can't tell me who he is, your head will fall off. Shakalya didn't know. And his head fell off: the text tells it in one plain sentence. Then one more grim line: thieves carried off his bones, thinking they were something else. Nothing more is said of him. How to hear this? The text doesn't explain. Some readers take it literally, as the real stake of these Vedic debates. Others hear it as an image: his whole argument came apart; he lost face, as people say now. Either way, set it beside Gargi. She got the very same warning, stopped, and came back later with better questions. Shakalya never stopped, and he was pushing as someone else's tool. Then the third book ends with a riddle. Yajnavalkya asks the room: a person is like a tree, hair for leaves, skin for bark. Cut a tree down, and it grows again from the root. From what root does a person grow, cut down by death? Nobody dares answer. The text answers instead: Brahman, which is knowing, which is joy.

382.title: Janaka and Yajnavalkya: what is the light of man? sun → moon → fire → speech → self (4.3)
382.hook: a king asks what light a person has, and takes the lights away one at a time
382.tomorrow: dreaming — the self creates its own world
382.howItsDone: Hindu homes and temples light lamps at dawn and dusk and at festivals, and teachers sometimes quote the Brihadaranyaka's line that the self is a person's own light when explaining the inner meaning of the lamp.

segments.voice: Yesterday: murdha, the head. Shakalya pushed past the limit as someone else's tool. Your line was don't ask past the limit.

The power goes out at night. The streetlights die, the screens go black, your phone is at one percent and then it's gone. You can't see your own hand. Then, from the next room, someone calls your name, and you get up and walk toward the voice. Something very like that moment is in the Brihadaranyaka, in a talk between a king and a sage with no crowd and no cows: King Janaka, asking one question and taking the lights away one by one.
screen: `THE POWER GOES OUT.` → `YOU CAN'T SEE YOUR HAND.` → `YOU WALK TOWARD THE VOICE.`

segments.voice: The debate is over. In book four, Yajnavalkya visits the king again, quietly. Yajnavalkya, Janaka asks, what light does a person have? The sun, your majesty. By the light of the sun a person sits, goes out, does their work, comes home. True. But when the sun has set, what light does a person have? The moon. And when the moon has set too? Fire. And when the fire has gone out? Speech. That's why, when you can't even see your own hand, wherever a voice is raised, you go toward it. True, Yajnavalkya. And when the sun and the moon have set, the fire has gone out, and speech has fallen silent, what light does a person have then? And Yajnavalkya says: atmaivasya jyotir bhavati. The self is their light. By the light of the self a person sits, goes out, does their work, comes home. Which is the self? The one made of knowing, among the senses, the light within the heart. Each light is real, and each one can go out. The question is what's left when all of them are gone. Sit in a dark room with your eyes open: nothing to look at, and still something knows it's dark. In the text's terms, that knowing is the self, the light under all the others.

383.title: Dreaming — the self creates its own world (4.3)
383.hook: there are no roads or chariots in a dream, and yet you ride one: who built it?
383.tomorrow: deep sleep — the embrace of the beloved
383.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers use the three states of waking, dream and deep sleep, laid out in this part of the Brihadaranyaka and in the Mandukya Upanishad, to point to the self that is present in all three.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jyotis. When the sun, moon, fire and speech are gone, the self is their light. Your line was your own light.

Last night, maybe, you were at a train station you've never seen. Someone who died years ago was there, talking normally. The house you grew up in had an extra room. Nobody built that station, and there's no train in your bedroom. So where did it come from, and what was lighting it, with your eyes closed in a dark room? Yajnavalkya, still talking with King Janaka, turns to the place a sleeper goes at night.
screen: `A STATION YOU'VE NEVER SEEN.` → `NO TRAIN IN YOUR BEDROOM.` → `WHO BUILT IT?`

segments.voice: A person has two places, Yajnavalkya says: this world, and the other world. And there's a third, where the two meet: sleep, dreaming. Standing there, you can see both. When a person dreams, he takes the material of this whole world, tears it down himself, builds it up himself, and dreams by his own brightness, by his own light. There, the person is his own light. Then the passage that gives today its line. There are no chariots there, no horses, no roads. But he makes chariots, horses, roads. There are no joys there, no pleasures, no delights. But he makes joys, pleasures, delights. There are no ponds, no lakes, no rivers. But he makes ponds, lakes, rivers. For he is the maker. Notice two things. First, the building material is borrowed: the station is made out of stations you've seen, the face out of faces you know. Nothing comes from nowhere. Second, the light. Yesterday, the self was the light left when every other light was gone. In the text, a dream is the proof: the room is dark, the eyes are shut, and still everything is lit. People see his playground, the text says, but nobody sees him. And a small, practical line: don't wake a sleeping person suddenly, people say; it's hard to heal someone who doesn't find their way back. Later Hindu schools argued over who really does the building in a dream, the dreamer or God, and what dreams say about waking. The Upanishad leaves it here: the dreamer builds.

384.title: Deep sleep — the embrace of the beloved (4.3)
384.hook: the best night's sleep you ever had, with nothing in it, and something that still woke up rested
384.tomorrow: death — the caterpillar reaching the next blade
384.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers use deep sleep, described here and in the Mandukya Upanishad, as an everyday clue to the self: something rests, and on waking, one knows one slept well.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dreaming. No chariots there, and the dreamer makes them, lit by his own light. Your line was the dreamer builds.

Some nights you sleep so deeply there's nothing to report. No dream, no time passing, no you. Then the alarm, and you sit up and say, I slept like a stone. It's the best sleep there is, and nobody was there to enjoy it. Or was there? Who, exactly, slept well? Yajnavalkya takes King Janaka one floor below the dreams, to the place you go every night and never remember.

segments.voice: As a falcon or an eagle, Yajnavalkya says, tired from circling all day in the sky, folds its wings and heads home to its nest, so a person hurries to that state where, asleep, he wants nothing and sees no dream. Then the image this day is named for. As a man held by the one he loves knows nothing outside and nothing inside, so a person held by the knowing self knows nothing outside and nothing inside. That is the form, the text says, where every desire is met, because the self is the only desire, so there's no desire at all, and no sorrow. Then a list that sounds almost dangerous. There, a father is not a father, a mother not a mother. Worlds are not worlds, gods are not gods. A thief is not a thief. Untouched by good, untouched by evil, he has crossed every sorrow of the heart. Nothing you are in daylight follows you in. And yet the text insists this isn't a blank. When he doesn't see there, he is still seeing, for the seer's seeing is never lost. There's just no second thing to see. A few weeks ago, in the Chandogya, Indra turned deep sleep down. In deep sleep, he worried, you don't even know yourself; it's like being destroyed. Here Yajnavalkya calls it an embrace. Both are in the Upanishads, and Hindu teachers have held them together ever since. The Mandukya, which you met last year, names this state prajna, the third of the self's four quarters, and points past it to a fourth.

385.title: Death — the caterpillar reaching the next blade (4.4)
385.hook: a small creature at the end of a blade of grass never lets go until it has hold of the next one
385.tomorrow: "as is his desire, so is his will; as his will, so his deed"
385.howItsDone: Hindu funeral rites, antyeshti, are performed by the family with fire and mantras, and the days that follow include offerings for the departed; passages like this one and Bhagavad Gita 2.22 may be read or recalled at the time of a death.

segments.voice: Yesterday: deep sleep, the falcon folding its wings, held with no inside and no outside. Your line was no inside, no outside.

Crouch down in a garden and watch a caterpillar climb a blade of grass. At the tip, it doesn't fall off, and it doesn't jump. It stretches its front end out into the air, waving a little, until it touches the next blade. It grips. Only then does it let go of the old one and draw the rest of itself across. Yajnavalkya and King Janaka have walked through waking, dreaming and deep sleep. Now the sage takes the last step, the one everyone takes, and he uses that caterpillar.
screen: `AT THE TIP OF A BLADE OF GRASS.` → `IT REACHES, AND GRIPS.` → `ONLY THEN DOES IT LET GO.`

segments.voice: First he describes the dying, gently and closely. The person grows weak and seems confused. The senses gather around the self, the way a king's officers gather when he's about to travel. The self draws all its powers in and goes down into the heart. People around the bed say: he doesn't see now, he doesn't hear now. He's becoming one. Then the tip of the heart lights up, and by that light the self leaves, and the breath and the senses follow. And what goes with it? What it knew, and what it did, and what it had lived. Then the picture. As a caterpillar, coming to the end of a blade of grass, reaches out to another and draws itself across, so the self, having laid down this body and let go of not-knowing, reaches out to another support and draws itself across. And one more: as a goldsmith takes a piece of gold and hammers it into another shape, newer and more beautiful, so the self makes itself another form. Notice what these pictures say. There's no gap in the caterpillar's crossing: it doesn't let go into nothing. And the gold is the same gold. You met Krishna's picture in the Gita last year, old clothes laid aside for new ones; it belongs to the same family. Look back at this week. Gargi's two arrows. The gods counted down to one. Shakalya's head. The light of the self. The dreamer building. Deep sleep's embrace. And today, the leaf.
screen: `THE SENSES GATHER; THE HEART LIGHTS UP.` · `WHAT IT KNEW, DID, AND LIVED GOES WITH IT.` · `THE CATERPILLAR REACHES THE NEXT BLADE.` · `THE GOLDSMITH'S GOLD, NEWLY SHAPED.` · then, large: `THE LEAF.`

segments.voice: At the very end of each out-breath, notice the tiny reach toward the next breath before the old one is quite finished; then let the old breath go, without hurrying it. If thoughts of death come, someone you've lost, or your own, let them be here too, and keep breathing through them, one blade to the next.
Death, as the Brihadaranyaka pictures it: a caterpillar at the tip of a blade of grass, reaching for the next before it lets go.
Your line: the leaf. The gold is still the same gold. Day three hundred eighty-five, done.
